newsitem.title: USA: Nuclear industry presses U.S. to take spent fuel.
newsitem.headline: Nuclear industry presses U.S. to take spent fuel.

text.p: U.S. nuclear utility executives Thursday urged Energy Secretary Federico Pena to take away the radioactive waste accumulating at their power plants next year, as the government is required to do by law.

In a 90-minute meeting, Pena and the industry officials did not discuss options the government had in mind to live up to its obligation to start taking the waste by February 1998 without having a dump for it, two executives said.
Some companies have said they might consider taking money from the government to pay for keeping the spent fuel on site until the Energy Department has a permanent dump ready.
But the issue of compensating nuclear utilities for having to store the nuclear waste beyond January 1998 was not discussed in depth at the meeting, the executives said.

"The industry's sole objective ... is to move fuel from reactor sites," said Joe Colvin, president of the Nuclear Energy Institute, which represents utilities that own nuclear plants. "That was the singular focus of the meeting."

Twentyseven nuclear units expect to run out of space in spent fuel pools by the end of January 1998. Pena agreed to explore what authority the government had to begin accepting fuel without having a permanent dump ready, Colvin said.
Yucca Mountain, Nevada is the only site being investigated for burying waste. Assuming a dump can be built, the Energy Department expects it to be ready in 2010 at the earliest.
"We believe they have the authority to begin to accept fuel," said Corbin McNeill, president and CEO of PECO Energy Co .
He said the government was already handling spent fuel from foreign research reactors and its own nuclear submarine reactors, and should be able to take power plant waste.

Several utilities and states are suing the government to start taking the waste on time, or stop requiring utilities to pay hundreds of millions of dollars a year into a federal fund which was meant to be used to build a nuclear waste dump.

Settlement of the lawsuit did not come up in the meeting with Pena, nor did legislation in Congress which would force the Clinton administration to build an interim storage site in Nevada, which the administration opposes.

Other top executives at the meeting were from Yankee Atomic Electric Co, Entergy Corp's Entergy Operations Inc, CMS Energy Corp, Texas Utilities Co's TU Electric, DTE Energy Co's Detroit Edison Co, Dominion Resources Inc's Virginia Power.
